AI & Community Banks: Friends or Foes?

VACB 49th Annual Convention · Charlottesville · October 2026

AI & Community Banks: Friends or Foes?

Practical AI, emerging risks, and the questions leaders should be asking

Chris Busse · SingleStone

Friends Foes

Wrong question

Neither. It isn’t a person.

Friend and foe are relationships. AI can’t have one with your bank: no loyalty, no grudge, no intent.

  • It is “an engineered or machine-based system that can, for a given set of objectives, generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions.”[1]
  • A language model stitches together language it has seen “without any reference to meaning.”[2]
  • So it can be fluent and wrong at once. NIST’s word for it is confabulation.[3]
a model, not a mind
  1. NIST (2023). AI Risk Management Framework 1.0, NIST AI 100-1, p. 1 & §5.
  2. Bender, Gebru, McMillan-Major & Shmitchell (2021). On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots. FAccT ’21, p. 617.
  3. NIST (2024). Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1, §2.

Not a foe

Most AI pilots don’t crash. They never leave the ground.

You’ve seen the headline: “95% of AI pilots fail.” Look under the cowling.

  • MIT’s own report: the gap is about approach, not model quality or regulation.[1]
  • What breaks is mechanical: brittle workflows, no one owning the result.[1]
  • RAND’s most common root cause: leadership “misunderstanding how to set the project on a pathway to success.”[2]

Hold the 95% loosely: a small, preliminary, self-reported study.[1]

grounded pilot
  1. Challapally et al., MIT NANDA (Jul. 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary findings).
  2. Ryseff, De Bruhl & Newberry, RAND (Aug. 2024). The Root Causes of Failure for AI Projects, RR-A2680-1.

But people can misuse it

The threat isn’t the tool. It’s who’s holding it.

  • FinCEN has seen “an increase in suspicious activity reporting … describing the suspected use of deepfake media in fraud schemes targeting their institutions and customers.”[1]
  • An Arup employee sent about US$25 million after a video call with deepfaked colleagues. Arup: “We can confirm that fake voices and images were used.”[2]
  • Deloitte projects generative AI could enable US fraud losses of $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023.[3]

Even here, the danger “comes not from the technology used to create it, but from people’s natural inclination to believe what they see.”[1]

Deepfake a person
  1. FinCEN (Nov. 13, 2024). Alert on Fraud Schemes Involving Deepfake Media Targeting Financial Institutions, FIN-2024-Alert004.
  2. Fortune (May 17, 2024). Arup confirms it was the victim of a HK$200M (US$25M) deepfake video-call fraud.
  3. Deloitte Center for Financial Services (May 29, 2024). Generative AI is expected to magnify the risk of deepfakes and other fraud in banking.

A tool can’t choose

Only a person decides — and a person answers.

“A computer can never be held accountable. Therefore a computer must never make a management decision.”[1]

  • Lawyers who filed ChatGPT’s invented cases were sanctioned: “existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys.”[2]
  • For banks: “A banking organization has ultimate responsibility…” — AI, vendor, or not.[3]

“There is no AI exemption to the laws on the books.” — then-FTC Chair Lina Khan, 2023.[4]

Approved by: a person

But if we must keep the metaphor…

AI is the friend who has every tool.

It will sell your bank one off the shelf — or help you build a new one.

Every tool.

Build it. Buy it. But you still have to pick one.

  1. “Knolling”: coined 1987 by Andrew Kromelow in Frank Gehry’s shop; popularized by Tom Sachs.

The real risk

Access isn’t the problem. Selection is.

“I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail.”[1]

The question isn’t “can AI do this?” It’s “which tool, for which job, under which controls?”

The tools are already in the building: 49% of banks say they have deployed generative AI.[2]

  1. Maslow, A. H. (1966). The Psychology of Science, pp. 15–16 (via Quote Investigator).
  2. Cornerstone Advisors (Jan. 29, 2026). What’s Going On in Banking 2026. n = 416 executives.

Practical applications

Start with the job, not the tool.

Three jobs AI does well at a community bank:

  • Efficiency loan-file intake, call and meeting summaries, first drafts of policies and procedures.
  • Customer service after-hours answers, call routing, an assistant at your front-line banker’s elbow.
  • Better decisions triaging fraud and BSA alerts, drafting credit memos, early warning across the portfolio.

AI for customer support is now a top opportunity for 47% of community bankers — up 16 points in a year.[1]

Efficiency Service Decisions
  1. CSBS (2025). 2025 CSBS Annual Survey of Community Banks, p. 17.

Finding the job

Walk the process before you pick the job.

Follow one loan file from application to close. Mark:

  • Waits where the file sits in a queue. The waiting usually dwarfs the work.[1]
  • Re-keying the same data typed into a second system.
  • Rework the file goes back for something missing.
  • Judgment where a person decides. AI can support it; it doesn’t take it.

The job for AI is usually a handoff or a re-key, not the whole process.[2]

Apply Intake Underwrite Close Rework Re-key Longest wait
  1. Rother & Shook (1999). Learning to See: Value Stream Mapping to Add Value and Eliminate Muda. Lean Enterprise Institute.
  2. Challapally et al., MIT NANDA (Jul. 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary findings).

Finding the job

Draw the walls: one job, one room.

Your bank already has walls: to deposits a customer is an account holder; to lending, a borrower; to BSA, a subject.[1] Give AI a job that fits in one:

  • One room one owner, one vocabulary, that room’s data only.
  • Through a door at a handoff you’ve mapped, not reaching into every room.
  • Worth doing high volume, a person already checking, a clear measure of better.

Software designers call these bounded contexts.[2] Pilots that sprawl across rooms stall on tools that “integrate poorly.”[3]

Depositscustomer = depositor BSA / AMLcustomer = risk subject Lendingcustomer = borrower
  1. Fowler (Jan. 15, 2014). BoundedContext. martinfowler.com.
  2. Evans (2003). Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. Addison-Wesley.
  3. Challapally et al., MIT NANDA (Jul. 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary findings).

Build or buy

Your friend can sell you a tool — or help you make one.

AI made small tools cheap to build. It did not make them cheap to own.

  • Buy what every bank needs: core, fraud, document intake. Your diligence is the control.
  • Build what’s yours alone, and small: an internal assistant, a workflow, a report. Then you are the vendor — testing, change control, support.

Lean towards buying: MIT found internal builds “fail twice as often.”[1] Most community banks already do.[2]

Build
  1. Challapally et al., MIT NANDA (Jul. 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary findings).
  2. U.S. Treasury (Mar. 2024). Managing AI-Specific Cybersecurity Risks in the Financial Services Sector.

If you buy

Buying the tool doesn’t sell off the risk.

“Use of third parties does not diminish banks’ responsibility to manage risks.”[1] Ask the vendor:

  • Is our customers’ data used to train your models?
  • How will you tell us when the model changes?
  • Can we explain its output to an examiner?
  • How do we leave?

Your core’s AI roadmap is your AI roadmap. The September 2026 proposal comes with a joint statement on community banks and their core providers.[1]

Buy
  1. FDIC FIL-58-2026 (Sept. 11, 2026). Proposed Interagency TPRM Guidance; Joint Statement on Core Service Providers.

Emerging risks

Match the tool to the risk.

  • Pencil drafting and summarizing. A person edits everything.
  • Drill customer-facing chat, copilots on internal data. You own what it says.[1]
  • Crane credit, fraud, BSA, pricing. Validation, fair-lending testing, and adverse-action reasons that are “specific.”[2]

Built or bought, the tier comes from the job, not the source. And the 2026 model-risk guidance puts generative and agentic AI out of scope[3] — build one, and those controls are yours to design.

Low Medium High

Emerging risks

Every tool gets only the data its job needs.

The safeguards didn’t change when the tools did.[1]

  • Any tool an approved list, and no customer information in consumer AI or personal accounts.
  • Bought by contract: no training on your data, retention you control, notice of a breach.
  • Built you’re the custodian: the least data the job needs, access controls, logs.
  • Every tool prompts and outputs are records.

And expect the fraud to come down-market, to “smaller institutions.”[2]

Customer data
  1. Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards: 12 CFR 364 App. B (FDIC); 30 App. B (OCC); 208 App. D-2 (Fed).
  2. U.S. Treasury (Mar. 2024). Managing AI-Specific Cybersecurity Risks in the Financial Services Sector.

Governance

Keep a human in the cockpit.

“Loop thinking creates blame cultures. Cockpit thinking creates ownership cultures.”[1]

  • Inventory every AI tool — including the ones inside vendor products.
  • Give each one a named pilot, and report to the board.
  • A person decides anything that affects a customer.
  • Watch the gauges: re-test when the vendor changes the model.

Right-size it. The OCC: its guidance “does not … require community banks to perform annual model validation.”[2] Examiners oversee AI with the rules they already have.[3]

Human in the cockpit
  1. Mishra, T. (n.d.). Time to retire “human-in-the-loop” and embrace “human-in-the-cockpit.” SingleStone.
  2. OCC Bulletin 2025-26 (Oct. 6, 2025). Model Risk Management: Clarification for Community Banks.
  3. GAO (May 2025). Artificial Intelligence: Use and Oversight in Financial Services, GAO-25-107197.

For the board table

Five questions leaders should be asking.

  1. Which jobs are we giving AI — have we walked the process, and who gets hurt if it’s wrong?
  2. Is this the lightest tool that does the job?
  3. Build or buy — and what do our vendors, and our core, do with our customers’ data?
  4. Could we explain the result to a customer and to an examiner?
  5. Who owns each AI tool, and how will we know when it drifts?
  1. Drawn from the sources cited throughout.
